q: You are at the helm, sailing with the wind over your right shoulder and the boom out to the left. Which tack are you on?
why: The tack is named after the side the wind comes over.

figure.note: Wind over the starboard side, boom to port

ru.Wind over the starboard side, boom to po: Ветер с правого борта, гик слева

q: From this point of sail you want to turn to sail downwind. Which way do you turn the boat?
answer: Bear away — turn the bow away from the wind
why: Bearing away takes you from close-hauled towards a run.

q: The boat is on this heading relative to the wind. What point of sail is it?
why: Wind on the beam, about 90° off the bow.

q: The boat is pointing into the shaded sector. What happens?
answer: The sails flap and the boat stops — it is the no-go zone
why: A yacht cannot sail closer than about 40–45° to the wind.

figure.note: Red sector: about 45° either side of the wind

ru.Red sector: about 45° either side of the: Красный сектор: около 45° в обе стороны от ветра

q: You are about to turn the stern through the wind on a run. What do you do first?
answer: Centre the mainsheet and warn the crew: "Gybe-ho"
why: A controlled gybe keeps the boom from slamming across.

q: You are sailing from Paros to Naxos on this heading. What point of sail are you on?
why: Wind on the quarter, about 135° off the bow, is a broad reach.

q: The genoa and main are sheeted in hard and you cannot steer any closer to the wind. What point of sail is this?
why: Close-hauled is the closest course to the wind that keeps the sails full, about 45°.

q: You were close-hauled and have borne away a little to this heading. What point of sail are you on now?
why: Between close-hauled (45°) and a beam reach (90°) is a close reach.

q: You settle on this heading for the long leg down to Kos. Where do you set the mainsail, and what is the main risk?
answer: Eased right out; an accidental gybe
why: On a run the main is eased fully, and a wind shift or wave can swing the boom across.

q: You have just borne away from close-hauled onto this heading. What do you do with the sheets?
answer: Ease both until the sails just stop luffing
why: As you bear away, ease the sheets: trim each sail to the edge of luffing.

q: You were close-hauled on 045°. Now the sails start to lift and flap. What has happened and what do you do?
answer: You are headed: bear away to keep the sails full
why: A veer of 20° puts 045° inside the no-go zone; bear away or tack.

q: The skipper calls "luff up 20 degrees". What heading do you steer?
why: Luffing up turns the bow towards the wind: 090° − 20° = 070°.

q: You bear away 45° from this heading. What is your new heading and point of sail?
why: Bearing away turns from the wind: 315° − 45° = 270°, wind now on the beam.

figure.note: Close-hauled, heading 315°, wind from the north

q: Your boat tacks through 90°. After tacking from this heading, what course will you be steering?
why: Close-hauled 45° each side of a northerly wind: 315° tacks to 045°.

figure.note: Close-hauled, heading 315°, wind from the north

q: Your destination is upwind, to the north-west. Which manoeuvre puts you on the other close-hauled course?
answer: Tack: turn the bow through the wind
why: Changing from one close-hauled course to the other means tacking.

q: On a dead run in light wind the genoa keeps collapsing behind the main. What can you do?
answer: Goose-wing it on the opposite side
why: Set the genoa on the side away from the main, ideally held out by a pole.

q: After a slow tack the boat has stopped like this and will not turn either way. What is it and what do you do?
answer: In irons: back the genoa to push the bow off
why: Head to wind with no way on; backing the headsail turns the bow.

q: You are sailing like this and the boat is rolling. How do you protect the crew?
answer: Rig a preventer, keep heads clear of the boom
why: An accidental gybe swings the boom across hard; a preventer holds it.

figure.note: Dead run in a swell, crew in the cockpit

ru.Dead run in a swell, crew in the cockpit: Чистый фордевинд на зыби, экипаж в кокпите

q: You are close-hauled as shown. What water track do you make?
why: Leeway pushes you downwind: wind on the port bow sets you to starboard, 040 + 5.

q: You are close-hauled under full main and genoa. The boat heels hard and fights the helm. What do you do?
answer: Reef now, before the wind builds further
why: Reef early — the first time you think of it, and well before F6 on a charter yacht.

figure.note: True wind rising 16 → 20 kn, weather helm

ru.True wind rising 16 → 20 kn, weather hel: Ист. ветер растёт 16 → 20 уз, яхта приводится

q: You have been running pleasantly under full sail for two hours. Now you must turn and beat back to harbour. What do you expect?
answer: Much more wind and spray — reef first
why: Downwind your boat speed is subtracted from the true wind; upwind it is added.

ru.Running · apparent wind 13 kn, sea easy: Фордевинд · вымпельный ветер 13 уз, волна небольшая
